money_at_stake.rationale: This candidate's own occurrence block carries no explicit anchor_date or window (unlike a signal card), so I snapped one myself per method section 0's UNDERWAY convention (year known, month not pinned to a specific dated act, so 2025-07-01) and note that as a limitation rather than presenting it as the card's own figure. On the money itself: I fetched all three cited sources myself this run. The Fortune article directly supports two figures: the industry must hire 349,000 more construction workers in 2026 (Associated Builders and Contractors) and AGC estimates 35 percent of construction workers are immigrants. The Eye On Housing (NAHB) analysis of 2024 Census data states foreign-born workers are 26.3 percent of the US construction workforce nationally (a record high), 42 percent in California, and 39 percent in Texas, with California and Texas each having more than half a million foreign-born construction workers. A prior draft of this appraisal rounded the national figure to 'approximately 30 percent' and an adversarial re-check correctly flagged that as a roughly 14 percent relative overstatement of the source's own 26.3 percent; this rationale now uses the source's stated figure throughout, and the evidence claim below quotes it exactly. The candidate record's own net-immigration pace figures (roughly 500,000 in 2025 declining to a projected 200,000 in 2026) and its farm-labor figures (about 70% of the US farm workforce foreign born, about 40% of hired crop labor undocumented) are not covered by any URL cited in this leg's evidence, so they are not folded into the money band; the net-immigration pace question is addressed under timing_fit, where I found two credible series that diverge from the card's framing and from each other. For the money band itself, applying the cited 26.3 percent national foreign-born construction-workforce share to the cited $2,166.5bn seasonally adjusted annual rate of US construction spending (June 2026) implies on the order of $570bn of annual construction activity performed by the workforce this occurrence directly shrinks, before counting agriculture at all (2,166.5 x 0.263 is approximately 570). That is a derived figure from two independently cited and quoted inputs, not a single published total, and it clears GT_100B by more than 5x even before agriculture is added; I found no cited dollar total for the farm sector this run so it is not folded into the number.

public_reach.rationale: The direct exposure, the wage bill and hiring gap in construction trades and the crop-labor gap in farming, sits overwhelmingly with private employers: small and mid-sized general contractors and subcontractors, and family or private farm operations. Neither of those categories is investable. A real second-order listed set exists on both sides: large public homebuilders and engineering and construction firms whose delivery schedules and trade-labor costs move with this shortage, and agricultural-equipment and harvest-automation makers, modular and prefabrication suppliers, and food processors on the substitution side. That is the 'split with a large unlisted share' anchor (40) rather than 'clearly reachable, mixed' (60): I found no citation this run putting a majority of the affected spend or labor at listed issuers, and the two sourced figures I have describe the shortage in terms of trades and undocumented-worker employment, not public-company exposure.

evidence.claim: An NBER working paper found employment among likely undocumented immigrants dropped 4 percent on average in areas with recent ICE raids, and construction was the most affected industry tracked, with employment dropping 7.5 percent.

evidence.source_excerpt: employment among likely undocumented immigrants dropped 4% on average in areas where ICE conducted recent raids. Construction was the most affected industry the researchers tracked, with employment dropping 7.5% for undocumented workers

capture_odds.rationale: Two capture stories, neither confirmed as a captured profit pool this run. On the cost side, a tighter trade-labor market raises wages and slows delivery for public homebuilders and E&C firms, which reads as a margin headwind rather than pricing power: the cited housing-starts figure shows volume already softening (down, not absorbing cost through higher throughput), and I have no citation this run showing homebuilders passing the cost through without demand loss. On the substitution side, harvest-automation and modular or prefabrication vendors have a plausible qualification-gated opportunity of the kind method section 3 rewards, but I found no citation this run sizing that opportunity or confirming pricing power for any named vendor. Scored at the 'some specs, mostly price-taker' anchor (40, placed slightly below at 38 given the cost-side evidence is stronger than the capture-side evidence) rather than higher.

evidence.claim: Construction workers broke ground on about 1.36 million homes last year, a 0.6 percent drop from 2024, while construction employment among likely undocumented workers fell 7.5 percent in areas with recent ICE enforcement raids, the largest drop of any industry the NBER researchers tracked.
evidence.source_name: Fortune, America's construction shortage collides with Trump's immigration crackdown
source_excerpt: Last year, construction workers broke ground on about 1.36 million homes, a 0.6% drop from 2024, according to data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis

employment among likely undocumented immigrants dropped 4% on average in areas where ICE conducted recent raids. Construction was the most affected industry the researchers tracked, with employment dropping 7.5% for undocumented workers

timing_fit.rationale: Measured against the anchor_date I derived (2025-07-01) and the repo's 2 to 5 year window (roughly 2027 to 2030 from as_of). Part of this is already committed and inside the window: the 349,000-worker 2026 hiring gap is a same-year figure, not a projection past the horizon, and the underlying labor contraction is independently confirmed as underway now (Census Bureau data show net international migration falling from 2.7 million in the year ending mid-2024 to 1.3 million in the year ending mid-2025, continuing to fall, with a further projected decline to about 321,000 in 2026). Scored at 'credible inside the window' (60) rather than higher because the candidate record's own pace figures (500,000 declining to 200,000) could not be confirmed against the Census series I fetched, which states a materially different pace, so how fast the contraction proceeds through the window is less certain than the card states; and because the chain-relevant downstream effects (accelerated automation or modular adoption, a visible repricing of listed homebuilders or E&C names) have not yet shown up in the cited data, so it is not yet clear how much of the eventual money movement lands inside 2 to 5 years versus playing out on a longer secular clock alongside the pre-existing structural aging of the trade workforce.

notes.text: The candidate's occurrence block cites a single Fortune URL for a bundle of figures, of which I could independently confirm only the 349,000-worker 2026 hiring gap and the 35 percent immigrant-labor AGC estimate directly inside that source after fetching it twice. The California/Texas 40 percent construction figure and the farm 70/40 figures are real and independently corroborated, but from other sources (NAHB/Eye On Housing and Southern Ag Today, the latter already named separately in the card's own occurrence_strength dimension), not from the cited URL. The card's specific net-immigration pace, 500,000 in 2025 to a projected 200,000 in 2026, does not match either credible series I found (Census Bureau net international migration: 2.7 million to 1.3 million to a projected roughly 321,000; Brookings/CBO net immigration of foreign nationals: negative 295,000 to negative 10,000 in 2025, negative 925,000 to positive 185,000 projected 2026). Both confirm a historic collapse in the same direction and broadly the same window, so I have not treated this as disqualifying, but I have scored timing_fit and flagged public_reach and capture_odds conservatively rather than resting on the card's own pace number. This occurrence also carries no explicit anchor_date or window unlike a signal card; I derived anchor_date 2025-07-01 from method section 0's UNDERWAY, year-known snapping convention and recorded that as a limitation rather than a fact on the card.

Re-verification pass after an adversarial fetch-check: I fetched all four cited URLs myself this run and added a verbatim source_excerpt to every evidence item. One item misread its own source: the Eye On Housing (NAHB) figure was rounded to 'approximately 30 percent' national foreign-born construction share when the source states 26.3 percent (a roughly 14 percent relative overstatement), and the California/Texas figures are exactly 42 percent and 39 percent rather than 'about 40 percent' for both. Both claims are corrected to quote the source's own numbers. The derived construction-spend-at-risk figure in money_at_stake.rationale moves from approximately $650bn to approximately $570bn (26.3% x $2,166.5bn); this does not change the GT_100B band, which the figure still clears by more than 5x, and does not change impact_score or impact_band (recomputed via tools/impact_score.py: 54.6, LEAKY, unchanged). The Census Bureau evidence item's source_date is corrected from the snapped 2026-01-01 to the page's actual publication date, 2026-01-27, and both the Census Bureau and Trading Economics evidence items were re-checked as primary-source fetches; the Census Bureau item is upgraded from INFERRED to VERIFIED as the primary publisher of its own migration estimate, fetched and quoted directly this run. No evidence item was deleted: all four cited URLs resolved and, once corrected to their own stated figures, support their claims. No leg moved to NULL.
